concepts: Determinant of adjoint and properties of determinants
Sum of an infinite G.P.
questions.question: $A_{3\times3}$ is a matrix such that $|A|=a$ and $B=\operatorname{adj}A$ is such that $|B|=b$. Find the value of $(ab^2+a^2b+1)S$, where $\frac12S=\frac ab+\frac{a^2}{b^3}+\frac{a^3}{b^5}+\cdots$ up to $\infty$, and $a=3$.
questions.key_idea: $|\operatorname{adj}A|=|A|^{n-1}=|A|^2$ for a $3\times3$ matrix, then the series is an infinite G.P.
solution: $\frac12S=\frac ab+\frac{a^2}{b^3}+\frac{a^3}{b^5}+\cdots$ is an infinite G.P. with first term $\frac ab=\frac13$ and common ratio $\frac a{b^2}=\frac3{81}=\frac1{27}$, which has modulus less than $1$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Keep $a,b$ symbolic with $b=a^2$: the factor $ab^2+a^2b+1=a^5+a^4+1$ factorises and cancels the denominator of $S$.
solution: Since $b=a^2$, the common ratio is $\frac a{b^2}=\frac1{a^3}$ and $\frac12S=\frac{a/b}{1-a/b^2}=\frac{1/a}{1-1/a^3}=\frac{a^2}{a^3-1}$, so $S=\frac{2a^2}{a^3-1}$.

useful_results: For an $n\times n$ matrix: $|\operatorname{adj}A|=|A|^{n-1}$, $|kA|=k^n|A|$, $|\operatorname{adj}(\operatorname{adj}A)|=|A|^{(n-1)^2}$.
Infinite G.P. with first term $t$ and ratio $r$: $S=\frac{t}{1-r}$, valid only for $|r|<1$.

concepts: Idempotent matrices and powers of a matrix
Telescoping infinite product
questions.question: Given the matrix $A=\begin{pmatrix}-1&3&5\\1&-3&-5\\-1&3&5\end{pmatrix}$ and $X$ the solution set of the equation $A^x=A$, where $x\in\mathbb N-\{1\}$. Evaluate $\prod\left(\frac{x^3+1}{x^3-1}\right)$ where the continued product extends over all $x\in X$.
questions.key_idea: $A^2=A$ makes every $x\ge2$ a solution, and $\frac{x^3+1}{x^3-1}$ splits into two telescoping products.
solution: So $A^2=A^3=A^4=\cdots=A$, and hence $x=2,3,4,5,\ldots$ (every natural number except $1$).

alternate_solutions.idea: $A$ has rank one, so $A^2=A$ follows from $\operatorname{tr}A=1$; then guess the partial product and prove it by induction.
solution: Every row of $A$ is $\pm(-1,3,5)$, so $A=wr^{T}$ with $w=(1,-1,1)^T$ and $r=(-1,3,5)^T$.

Induction step: the conjecture gives $\frac{P_n}{P_{n-1}}=\frac{3n(n+1)}{2(n^2+n+1)}\cdot\frac{2(n^2-n+1)}{3(n-1)n}=\frac{(n+1)(n^2-n+1)}{(n-1)(n^2+n+1)}=\frac{n^3+1}{n^3-1}$, exactly the next factor.

useful_results: A rank-one matrix $A=wr^T$ satisfies $A^n=(r^Tw)^{n-1}A$; it is idempotent exactly when $r^Tw=\operatorname{tr}A=1$.
Telescoping pattern: with $f(x)=x^2-x+1$ we have $f(x+1)=x^2+x+1$, so $\prod_{x=2}^n\frac{f(x)}{f(x+1)}=\frac{f(2)}{f(n+1)}$.
$\prod_{n=2}^\infty\frac{n^3-1}{n^3+1}=\frac23$ (and its reciprocal $\frac32$); the same splitting works for $\frac{n^3-1}{n^3+1}$ in any 'cube' product.
For $x^3\pm1$ always factor first: $x^3-1=(x-1)(x^2+x+1)$, $x^3+1=(x+1)(x^2-x+1)$.

concepts: Orthogonal and skew-symmetric matrices; inverse of a matrix
questions.question: If $A$ is a skew-symmetric matrix and $I+A$ is non-singular, then prove that the matrix $B=(I-A)(I+A)^{-1}$ is an orthogonal matrix. Use this to find a matrix $B$ given $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&5\\-5&0\end{pmatrix}$.
questions.key_idea: $(I+A)^T=I-A$, so $B^T=(I-A)^{-1}(I+A)$ and the factors cancel in $B^TB$.
solution: $(I+A)$ and $(I-A)$ commute, so $B^TB=(I-A)^{-1}(I-A)(I+A)(I+A)^{-1}=I\cdot I=I$. Hence $B$ is an orthogonal matrix.

alternate_solutions.idea: Show that $B$ preserves lengths using $y^TAy=0$ for skew $A$; for the $2\times2$ case treat $A=5J$ like the complex number $5i$ and use $\frac{1-5i}{1+5i}$.
solution: Take any vector $x$ and put $y=(I+A)^{-1}x$, so $x=(I+A)y$ and $Bx=(I-A)y$.
So $\|Bx\|=\|(I-A)y\|=\|(I+A)y\|=\|x\|$ for every $x$: $B$ preserves lengths, which means $B^TB=I$ ($B$ is orthogonal).
For the $2\times2$ part write $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$ ($J^2=-I$), so $A=5J$ behaves like the complex number $5i$ and $a+bJ\leftrightarrow a+bi$.

useful_results: Cayley transform: for real skew-symmetric $A$, $(I-A)(I+A)^{-1}$ is orthogonal with determinant $+1$ (here $\frac{144+25}{169}=1$).
For real skew-symmetric $A$, $I+A$ is always invertible, because $x^TAx=0$ gives $x^T(I+A)x=\|x\|^2>0$ for $x\neq0$.
$2\times2$ rotations: $\begin{pmatrix}p&q\\-q&p\end{pmatrix}\leftrightarrow p+qi$; products and inverses are then complex arithmetic, and $\frac{1-ti}{1+ti}=e^{-2i\tan^{-1}t}$.
A matrix $B$ is orthogonal $\iff B^TB=I\iff$ it preserves lengths $\|Bx\|=\|x\|$.

concepts: Inverse of a matrix and solving a matrix equation
questions.question: Given that $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&2\\2&2&3\\1&-1&3\end{pmatrix}$, $C=\begin{pmatrix}2&1&1\\2&2&1\\1&1&1\end{pmatrix}$, $D=\begin{pmatrix}10\\13\\9\end{pmatrix}$ and that $CB=D$. Solve the matrix equation $Ax=B$.
questions.key_idea: Multiply $Ax=B$ by $C$: $CAx=CB=D$, so $x=(CA)^{-1}D$ and $B$ is never needed.

alternate_solutions.idea: Find $B$ first by subtracting the three equations of $CB=D$, then solve $Ax=B$ by elimination; no $3\times3$ inverse is needed.
solution: Second minus first: $b_2=3$. First minus third: $b_1=1$. Then $b_3=9-1-3=5$, so $B=(1,3,5)^T$.
Second minus first: $x_1+x_3=2$, so $x_1=2-x_3$. Put it in the first: $2x_2+x_3=-1$. Put it in the third: $-x_2+2x_3=3$.

useful_results: If $CB=D$ and $Ax=B$, then $(CA)x=D$: premultiply, do not solve for the intermediate matrix unless it is easy.
A $3\times3$ inverse is costly; Gauss elimination on $[M\,|\,D]$ is usually faster and less error-prone.
Always verify by substituting back into the original system (here $A(1,-1,1)^T=(1,3,5)^T=B$).
$(CA)^{-1}=A^{-1}C^{-1}$ (reverse order) when both $A,C$ are invertible.

concepts: Cayley–Hamilton theorem and inverse of a $2\times2$ matrix
questions.question: If $A=\begin{pmatrix}k&m\\\ell&n\end{pmatrix}$ and $kn\neq\ell m$, then show that $A^2-(k+n)A+(kn-\ell m)I=O$. Hence find $A^{-1}$.
questions.key_idea: A matrix satisfies its own characteristic equation; multiplying that equation by $A^{-1}$ isolates $A^{-1}$.
solution: The characteristic equation of $A$ is $|A-\lambda I|=0$, i.e. $\begin{vmatrix}k-\lambda&m\\\ell&n-\lambda\end{vmatrix}=0$.
By the Cayley–Hamilton theorem, $A$ satisfies its characteristic equation (put $\lambda=A$): $A^2-(k+n)A+(kn-\ell m)I=O$.
Since $|A|=kn-\ell m\neq0$, $A^{-1}$ exists. Multiply the relation by $A^{-1}$: $A-(k+n)I+(kn-\ell m)A^{-1}=O$.
questions.correction_note: PDF solution stops after writing the characteristic equation and 'Put lambda = A'. It does not show the identity holds for A (it is quoted from Cayley-Hamilton) and never finds A^-1. Steps for multiplying by A^-1 and the final inverse were added; nothing in the PDF was wrong.

alternate_solutions.idea: Do not quote the theorem: multiply out $A^2$ directly, then get $A^{-1}$ from the adjoint formula and check it against the identity.
solution: Adjoint method: the cofactors of $A$ give $\operatorname{adj}A=\begin{pmatrix}n&-m\\-\ell&k\end{pmatrix}$ and $|A|=kn-\ell m\neq0$.

useful_results: For every $2\times2$ matrix: $A^2-(\operatorname{tr}A)A+(\det A)I=O$, and so $A^{-1}=\frac{(\operatorname{tr}A)I-A}{\det A}$ when $\det A\neq0$.
Cayley–Hamilton lets you reduce high powers: from $A^2=(\operatorname{tr}A)A-(\det A)I$ every $A^n$ equals $pA+qI$.
For $3\times3$: $A^3-(\operatorname{tr}A)A^2+cA-(\det A)I=O$ where $c$ is the sum of principal $2\times2$ minors.
Check on $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{pmatrix}$: $A^2=\begin{pmatrix}7&10\\15&22\end{pmatrix}=5A+2I$ and $\operatorname{tr}A=5$, $\det A=-2$ (so $A^2-5A-2I=O$).

concepts: Matrix equations with singular matrices ($AX=A$, $XA=I$, $XB=O$)
questions.question: Given $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\2&1\end{pmatrix}$, $B=\begin{pmatrix}9&3\\3&1\end{pmatrix}$; $I$ is the unit matrix of order $2$. Find all possible matrices $X$ in the following cases: (i) $AX=A$  (ii) $XA=I$  (iii) $XB=O$ but $BX\neq O$.
questions.key_idea: Both $A$ and $B$ are singular, so nothing can be cancelled: write $X=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$ and compare entries.
solution: So $2a+c=2$, i.e. $c=2(1-a)$ with $a\in\mathbb R$, and $2b+d=1$, i.e. $d=1-2b$ with $b\in\mathbb R$. Hence $X=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\2-2a&1-2b\end{pmatrix}$.

(ii) $XA=I$ gives $\begin{pmatrix}2(a+b)&a+b\\2(c+d)&c+d\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, which is not possible (the $(1,2)$ entry gives $a+b=0$ but then the $(1,1)$ entry is $0\neq1$). So $X$ does not exist.
(iii) $XB=O$ gives $\begin{pmatrix}3(3a+b)&3a+b\\3(3c+d)&3c+d\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$, so $3a+b=0$ and $3c+d=0$, i.e. $b=-3a$, $d=-3c$ with $a,c\in\mathbb R$.
With $b=-3a$, $d=-3c$ we get $3b+d=-3(3a+c)$, so both conditions say the same: $3a+c\neq0$. Hence $X=\begin{pmatrix}a&-3a\\c&-3c\end{pmatrix}$ with $3a+c\neq0$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Factor the rank-one matrices: $A=uv^T$ and $B=ww^T$; then each equation says something about one row or column of $X$.
solution: (i) $AX=u(v^TX)$. The equation $u(v^TX)=uv^T$ means $v^TX=v^T$: $(2\ \ 1)X=(2\ \ 1)$, so $2a+c=2$ and $2b+d=1$. This is the same family as before.
(ii) $XA=(Xu)v^T$ has rank at most $1$, but $I$ has rank $2$, so $XA=I$ is impossible.

$BX=w(w^TX)
eq O\iff w^TX
eq0\iff(3a+c,\ 3b+d)
eq(0,0)$, i.e. $3a+c
eq0$, since $3b+d=-3(3a+c)$. Same answer.

useful_results: A rank-one matrix is $uv^T$; then $uv^TX=u(v^TX)$ and $Xuv^T=(Xu)v^T$, which turns matrix equations into equations on one row or one column.
If $A$ is singular, $AX=AY$ does not imply $X=Y$: matrices have zero divisors, so cancellation fails.
$XA=I$ (or $AX=I$) is impossible whenever $\operatorname{rank}A<n$, because $\operatorname{rank}(XA)\le\operatorname{rank}A$.
Cases like $XB=O$ but $BX\neq O$ show matrix multiplication is not commutative.

concepts: Product of matrices and solving a system of equations using the inverse
questions.question: Find the product of two matrices $A$ and $B$, where $A=\begin{pmatrix}-5&1&3\\7&1&-5\\1&-1&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $B=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&2\\3&2&1\\2&1&3\end{pmatrix}$, and use it to solve the following system of linear equations: $x+y+2z=1;\ 3x+2y+z=7;\ 2x+y+3z=2$.
questions.key_idea: $AB=4I$ gives $B^{-1}=\frac14A$ without any inversion, and the coefficient matrix of the system is $B$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Solve the system by plain elimination (no matrices): two differences give $x+z$ and $x-3z$ at once.

useful_results: If $AB=kI$ with $k\neq0$, then $A^{-1}=\frac1kB$ and $B^{-1}=\frac1kA$; products like this are designed so that no inversion is required.
A system $BX=C$ is solved by $X=B^{-1}C$; for $3\times3$, direct elimination is an equally good check.
Here $A=4B^{-1}=-\operatorname{adj}B$, because $\operatorname{adj}B=|B|B^{-1}$ and $|B|=-4$; so such a product can also be read from the cofactors.
Always check a solution in at least two of the original equations.

concepts: Zero divisors in matrices: non-zero $X$ with $AX=O$; non-commutativity
questions.question: If $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{pmatrix}$, then find a non-zero square matrix $X$ of order $2$ such that $AX=O$. Is $XA=O$? If $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&3\end{pmatrix}$, is it possible to find a square matrix $X$ such that $AX=O$? Give reasons for it.
questions.answer: $X=\begin{pmatrix}-2c&-2d\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$ ($c,d$ not both $0$); $XA=O$ only if $c+2d=0$, so in general $XA\neq O$; for the second $A$ only $X=O$ works (no non-zero $X$)
questions.key_idea: The rows of the first $A$ are proportional, so $AX=O$ has non-zero solutions; the second $A$ has $|A|\neq0$, so it can be cancelled.
solution: The second row is twice the first, so only two equations remain: $a+2c=0$ and $b+2d=0$.
$X=\begin{pmatrix}-2c&-2d\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$, where $c,d\in\mathbb R$ are not both zero (so that $X\neq O$).
This is $O$ only when $c+2d=0$; for example $c=1,d=0$ gives $XA\neq O$. So $XA=O$ does not follow from $AX=O$: in general, no.
$AX=O\Rightarrow X=A^{-1}O=O$. So no non-zero square matrix $X$ satisfies $AX=O$ (only the zero matrix does).
questions.correction_note: PDF writes XA = [[-2c,-2d],[c,d]][[1,2],[2,4]] != 0 and answers 'NO'; it is nonzero only in general (XA = (c+2d)[[-2,-4],[1,2]] vanishes when c+2d = 0). The PDF also gives no working for the second matrix A = [[1,2],[2,3]]; its determinant is -1, so only X = O exists. Both added.

alternate_solutions.idea: Kernel viewpoint: every column of $X$ must lie in the null space of $A$, so $X=nw^T$ with $n=(-2,1)^T$; then $XA=n(w^TA)$ is easy.
solution: $AX=O$ means each column of $X$ is a solution of $Ay=0$, i.e. $y_1+2y_2=0$: $y=t(-2,1)^T$. So the null space of $A$ is spanned by $n=(-2,1)^T$.
$XA=n(w^TA)=n\,(c+2d,\ 2c+4d)=(c+2d)\,n\,(1,2)$, which is $O$ iff $c+2d=0$. So in general $XA\neq O$.
For $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&3\end{pmatrix}$ the null space is $\{0\}$, because the rows are not proportional ($|A|=-1$), so every column of $X$ is $0$ and $X=O$. Same answer.

useful_results: A square matrix $A$ has a non-zero $X$ with $AX=O$ if and only if $|A|=0$ (matrices have zero divisors).
$AX=O$ does not imply $XA=O$; but if $|A|\neq0$ then $AX=O$ or $XA=O$ forces $X=O$.
For singular $2\times2$ $A$, all solutions of $AX=O$ are $X=nw^T$ with $n$ spanning $\ker A$ and $w$ arbitrary.
Rows proportional $\Rightarrow$ $|A|=0$ $\Rightarrow$ the system $Ay=0$ has infinitely many solutions.

concepts: System of linear equations: unique, no and infinitely many solutions
questions.question: Determine the values of $a$ and $b$ for which the system $\begin{pmatrix}3&-2&1\\5&-8&9\\2&1&a\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\\z\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}b\\3\\-1\end{pmatrix}$ (i) has a unique solution; (ii) has no solution; (iii) has infinitely many solutions.
questions.key_idea: Unique solution iff $\Delta\neq0$; when $\Delta=0$ compare a Cramer determinant ($\Delta_1$) with $0$ and check the rank for the infinite case.
solution:
(i) Unique solution: $\Delta
eq0$, i.e. $-14a-42
eq0$, so $a
eq-3$ and $b\in\mathbb R$.
(ii) For no solution $\Delta=0$, so $a=-3$, and at least one of the other determinants must be non-zero.
So there is no solution when $a=-3$ and $b\neq\frac13$.
(iii) For infinitely many solutions $a=-3$ and $\Delta_1=0$, i.e. $b=\frac13$.

Check that the system is then consistent: for $a=-3$ the third row combination $3R_1-2R_3=(5,-8,9)=R_2$, and $3b-2(-1)=3\Rightarrow b=\frac13$, so the rank is $2<3$ and there are infinitely many solutions.
questions.correction_note: PDF (iii) simply states a = -3, b = 1/3 after (ii). For a singular system a zero value of one determinant Delta_1 is only necessary for consistency; a rank/row-relation check was added (R2 = 3R1 - 2R3 and RHS 3 = 3b + 2 at b = 1/3). The PDF's results for (i)-(iii) are all correct.

alternate_solutions.idea: For $a=-3$ find the dependency among the rows ($R_2=3R_1-2R_3$); the right-hand sides must obey the same relation.
solution: $\Delta=-14(a+3)$, so for $a\neq-3$ the system has a unique solution for every $b$: (i).
So $R_2=3R_1-2R_3$. A solution exists only if the right-hand sides satisfy the same relation: $3=3(b)-2(-1)=3b+2$, i.e. $b=\frac13$.
If $b\neq\frac13$ the relation fails: $0=3-(3b+2)\neq0$, so the equations contradict each other: no solution (ii).
If $b=\frac13$ the third equation is a combination of the other two (rank $2$): one free variable, infinitely many solutions (iii). Same answers.

useful_results: For $A\mathbf x=\mathbf b$ with $|A|=0$: if the rows satisfy a relation $\sum p_iR_i=0$, the system is consistent iff $\sum p_ib_i=0$ with the same $p_i$.
Rank test: unique if $\rho(A)=\rho(A|b)=n$; infinite if $\rho(A)=\rho(A|b)<n$; none if $\rho(A)<\rho(A|b)$.
If $|A|=0$ and some Cramer determinant $\Delta_i\neq0$, there is no solution; $\Delta_i=0$ for all $i$ is necessary for infinitely many solutions but is not by itself sufficient.
Expanding a $3\times3$ determinant along the row/column with the parameter keeps the algebra short.

concepts: Matrix equations and inverse of a $2\times2$ matrix
questions.question: If $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{pmatrix}$, $B=\begin{pmatrix}3&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, $C=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{pmatrix}$ and $X=\begin{pmatrix}x_1&x_2\\x_3&x_4\end{pmatrix}$, then solve the following matrix equations: (a) $AX=B-I$  (b) $(B-I)X=IC$  (c) $CX=A$.
questions.key_idea: Premultiply by the inverse when the matrix is invertible; for the singular $C$ the determinant rule $|C||X|=|A|$ shows there is no solution.
solution: (c) $CX=A$. Here $|C|=4-4=0$, so $C^{-1}$ does not exist and $X=C^{-1}A$ cannot be formed.
If a solution existed, $|C||X|=|A|$ would give $0=-2$, a contradiction. So $CX=A$ has no solution.
questions.correction_note: PDF (c): 'Inverse is not possible as |C| = 0' - this only shows the method X = C^-1 A fails, not that no X exists (e.g. CX = O has solutions). The argument |C||X| = |A| (0 = -2, impossible) was added. (a) and (b) are correct as printed.

alternate_solutions.idea: Gauss–Jordan on the augmented matrix $[M\,|\,R]$ solves $MX=R$ without computing an inverse, and shows the inconsistency in (c) at once.
solution: (c) $[C\,|\,A]=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&1&2\\2&4&3&4\end{pmatrix}$. $R_2-2R_1$: $(0\ 0\ 1\ 0)$, i.e. $0\cdot x_1+0\cdot x_3=1$ in the first column: impossible.
So (c) has no solution. Same answers.

useful_results: To solve $MX=R$ row-reduce $[M\,|\,R]$ to $[I\,|\,M^{-1}R]$; this solves all columns of $X$ at once.
$MX=R$ with singular $M$ is solvable only if the rows of $R$ obey the same dependencies as the rows of $M$; the test $|M||X|=|R|$ rules out $|R|\neq0$ at once.
For $XM=R$ transpose: $M^TX^T=R^T$, or use $X=RM^{-1}$ (order matters).
$2\times2$ inverse: $\begin{pmatrix}p&q\\r&s\end{pmatrix}^{-1}=\frac1{ps-qr}\begin{pmatrix}s&-q\\-r&p\end{pmatrix}$.

concepts: Orthogonal matrices and their properties
questions.question: If $A$ is an orthogonal matrix and $B=AP$ where $P$ is a non-singular matrix, then show that the matrix $PB^{-1}$ is also orthogonal.

alternate_solutions.idea: Simplify $PB^{-1}$ first: it is just $A^{-1}=A^T$, and the inverse of an orthogonal matrix is orthogonal.
solution: Hence $PB^{-1}=A^T$ is orthogonal. Same conclusion in one line.

useful_results: Orthogonal matrices form a group: products, inverses and transposes of orthogonal matrices are orthogonal; $\det=\pm1$.
For invertible $P$: $P(AP)^{-1}=A^{-1}$; always simplify products like $PB^{-1}$ before computing transposes.
$A$ orthogonal $\iff A^TA=AA^T=I\iff$ rows (and columns) are orthonormal.

concepts: Consistency of a linear system using determinants (Cramer's rule)
questions.question: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}a&1&0\\1&b&d\\1&b&c\end{pmatrix}$, $B=\begin{pmatrix}a&1&1\\0&d&c\\f&g&h\end{pmatrix}$, $U=\begin{pmatrix}f\\g\\h\end{pmatrix}$, $V=\begin{pmatrix}a^2\\0\\0\end{pmatrix}$, $X=\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\\z\end{pmatrix}$. If $AX=U$ has infinitely many solutions, then prove that $BX=V$ cannot have a unique solution. If further $afd\neq0$, then prove that $BX=V$ has no solution.
questions.key_idea: The condition $\Delta_2=0$ for $AX=U$ is exactly $|B|=0$, because $B^T$ is $\Delta_2$ with two columns interchanged.
solution: $AX=U$ has infinitely many solutions, so $|A|=0$ and every $\Delta_i=0$, where $\Delta_i$ is $|A|$ with its $i$th column replaced by $U$.
Since $|B|=0$, the system $BX=V$ cannot have a unique solution.

For $BX=V$ the determinant with the 2nd column replaced by $V$ is $\Delta_2'=\begin{vmatrix}a&a^2&1\\0&0&c\\f&0&h\end{vmatrix}=a^2cf$, and with the 3rd column replaced it is $\Delta_3'=\begin{vmatrix}a&1&a^2\\0&d&0\\f&g&0\end{vmatrix}=-a^2df$.
If $afd\neq0$ then $\Delta_3'=-a^2df\neq0$ while $|B|=0$. Hence $BX=V$ has no solution.
questions.correction_note: PDF derives g = h and c = d from the conditions on A and then says columns C2 and C3 of B are identical. That is not forced: ab = 1, c != d, g != h is possible (a=b=1,c=2,d=1,f=1,g=2,h=3: AX=U has infinitely many solutions yet g != h), so the argument is incomplete. The PDF also writes |B3| = +a^2 d f; the correct value is -a^2 d f (still non-zero). Replaced by the general identity |B| = -Delta_2, which holds under the stated hypothesis.

alternate_solutions.idea: Eliminate $x$ from $BX=V$: the remaining $2\times2$ system has proportional left sides but a non-zero right side, because $|B|=-\Delta_2=0$.
solution: As before, infinitely many solutions of $AX=U$ force $\Delta_2=a(cg-dh)-f(c-d)=0$, i.e. $|B|=-\Delta_2=0$: $BX=V$ has no unique solution.
Now let $afd\neq0$ and suppose $BX=V$ had a solution: $ax+y+z=a^2$, $dy+cz=0$, $fx+gy+hz=0$.
The determinant of $\begin{pmatrix}f-ag&f-ah\\d&c\end{pmatrix}$ is $(f-ag)c-(f-ah)d=f(c-d)-a(cg-dh)=-\Delta_2=0$, so (as $d\neq0$) $(f-ag,\ f-ah)=k(d,c)$ with $k=\frac{f-ag}{d}$.
Then the left side of the eliminated equation equals $k(dy+cz)=k\cdot0=0$, but its right side is $a^2f\neq0$. Contradiction, so $BX=V$ has no solution. Same conclusion.

useful_results: If $AX=U$ is consistent and $|A|=0$, every $\Delta_i=0$ (Cramer); conversely, if $|A|=0$ and some $\Delta_i\neq0$ the system has no solution.
Interchanging two columns changes the sign of a determinant and $|M^T|=|M|$: look for a rearrangement that turns one determinant into another.
$|A|$ for $\begin{pmatrix}a&1&0\\1&b&d\\1&b&c\end{pmatrix}$ factors as $(c-d)(ab-1)$ because rows $2,3$ differ only in the last entry.
Infinite solutions of $AX=U$ (with $|A|=0$) need more than $|A|=0$; do not assume stronger conditions (like $g=h$) than the determinants give.

concepts: Orthogonal rows of a $2\times2$ matrix
Counting of matrices with entries $\pm1$
questions.question: Find the number of $2\times2$ matrices satisfying: (i) $a_{ij}$ is $1$ or $-1$; (ii) $a_{11}^2+a_{12}^2=a_{21}^2+a_{22}^2=2$; (iii) $a_{11}a_{21}+a_{12}a_{22}=0$.
questions.key_idea: With entries $\pm1$ condition (ii) is automatic, and (iii) says the two products $a_{11}a_{21}$, $a_{12}a_{22}$ are opposite.
solution: (iii) $a_{11}a_{21}+a_{12}a_{22}=0$: each product is $\pm1$, so they must be equal and opposite: $a_{12}a_{22}=-a_{11}a_{21}$.
Choose $a_{11},a_{21},a_{12}$ freely ($2\cdot2\cdot2=8$ ways). Then $a_{22}=-\frac{a_{11}a_{21}}{a_{12}}$ is forced and is $\pm1$.
Hence there are $8$ such matrices (equivalently $4\times2=8$: four choices for the first row, then two orthogonal second rows).

alternate_solutions.idea: Condition (ii)–(iii) says $\frac1{\sqrt2}A$ is an orthogonal matrix; the orthogonal $2\times2$ matrices with all entries $\pm\frac1{\sqrt2}$ are rotations and reflections by odd multiples of $45^\circ$.
solution: (ii) and (iii) say the rows of $A$ are orthogonal vectors of length $\sqrt2$, so $\frac1{\sqrt2}A$ is an orthogonal matrix with all entries $\pm\frac1{\sqrt2}$.

Every $2\times2$ orthogonal matrix is a rotation $\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\\sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{pmatrix}$ or a reflection $\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta&\sin\theta\\\sin\theta&-\cos\theta\end{pmatrix}$.
All entries have modulus $\frac1{\sqrt2}$ iff $|\cos\theta|=|\sin\theta|$, i.e. $\theta=45^\circ,135^\circ,225^\circ,315^\circ$: $4$ values.
That gives $4$ rotations and $4$ reflections, in total $8$ matrices. Same answer.

useful_results: A $2\times2$ matrix with entries $\pm1$ and orthogonal rows is a (scaled) orthogonal matrix: a Hadamard matrix of order $2$; there are exactly $8$.
For $\pm1$ entries, 'dot product $=0$' means the products $x_iy_i$ must cancel: an even number of terms is needed (Hadamard matrices exist only for orders $1,2,4k$).
Counting recipe: choose as many free entries as possible, then check the constraint fixes the rest uniquely.
Orthogonal $2\times2$: rotations (det $1$) and reflections (det $-1$) — two one-parameter families.

concepts: Matrix equation $AB=B$ and determinant of a $2\times2$ matrix
questions.question: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$ and $B=\begin{pmatrix}p\\q\end{pmatrix}\neq\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\end{pmatrix}$, such that $AB=B$ and $a+d=5050$. Find the value of $(ad-bc)$.
questions.key_idea: $AB=B$ with $B\neq0$ means $(A-I)B=0$ has a non-zero solution, so $\det(A-I)=0$.
solution: Multiply (1) by $(1-d)$ and use (2): $b\,(1-d)q=bcp$, so $bcp=p(1-a)(1-d)$, i.e. $p\left[bc-(1-a)(1-d)\right]=0$.
questions.correction_note: PDF divides (1) by (2) to get b/(1-d) = (1-a)/c, which is not allowed unless p, q, c and 1-d are non-zero; none of this is given. The step was replaced by multiplying through, giving p[bc-(1-a)(1-d)] = 0 and q[...] = 0, with (p,q) != (0,0). Final answer 5049 unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Eigenvalue view: $B\neq0$ with $AB=B$ means $1$ is an eigenvalue of $A$; the trace gives the other eigenvalue and the determinant is their product.
solution: $(A-I)B=O$ with $B\neq0$, so $A-I$ is singular: $1$ is an eigenvalue of $A$.
The two eigenvalues of $A$ add up to $\operatorname{tr}A=a+d=5050$, so the other eigenvalue is $5050-1=5049$.

useful_results: If $AB=B$ with $B\neq0$ then $1$ is an eigenvalue of $A$, so $\det(A-I)=0$; in general $A\mathbf v=\lambda\mathbf v$, $\mathbf v\neq0\Rightarrow\det(A-\lambda I)=0$.
For $2\times2$: $\det(A-I)=\det A-\operatorname{tr}A+1$, so '$1$ is an eigenvalue' means $\det A=\operatorname{tr}A-1$.
$\lambda_1+\lambda_2=\operatorname{tr}A$ and $\lambda_1\lambda_2=\det A$ for a $2\times2$ matrix.
Divide an equation only after you know the divisor is non-zero; multiply cross-wise instead.

concepts: Commutativity of matrices
questions.question: If the matrices $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{pmatrix}$ and $B=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$ ($a,b,c,d$ not all simultaneously zero) commute, find the value of $\frac{d-b}{a+c-b}$. Also show that the matrix which commutes with $A$ is of the form $\begin{pmatrix}\alpha-\beta&2\beta/3\\\beta&\alpha\end{pmatrix}$.
questions.key_idea: $AB=BA$ gives only two independent relations, $2c=3b$ and $c=d-a$, which make numerator and denominator equal.

alternate_solutions.idea: For a non-scalar $2\times2$ matrix $A$, every matrix commuting with $A$ is a polynomial in $A$: $B=xA+yI$.
solution: Matrices commuting with the non-scalar matrix $A$ are exactly $B=xA+yI$ ($x,y$ real). Reason: $A$ has distinct eigenvalues, and $B$ must share its eigenvectors.

useful_results: For a non-scalar $2\times2$ matrix $A$, $\{B:AB=BA\}=\{xA+yI\}$, a two-dimensional space; the commutation equations have rank $2$, not $4$.
If $AB=BA$ and $A$ has distinct eigenvalues, $A$ and $B$ have the same eigenvectors.
Matrices commuting with $\begin{pmatrix}p&q\\r&s\end{pmatrix}$: $B=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$ satisfies $rb=qc$ and $q(d-a)=b(s-p)$.
Relations from commutation often make several expressions proportional: look for common factors before computing.

concepts: Determinant, adjoint and skew-symmetric matrix of odd order
questions.question: Let $k$ be a positive real number and let $A=\begin{pmatrix}2k-1&2\sqrt k&2\sqrt k\\2\sqrt k&1&-2k\\-2\sqrt k&2k&-1\end{pmatrix}$ and $B=\begin{pmatrix}0&2k-1&\sqrt k\\1-2k&0&2\sqrt k\\-\sqrt k&-2\sqrt k&0\end{pmatrix}$. If $\det(\operatorname{adj}A)+\det(\operatorname{adj}B)=10^6$, then $[k]$ is equal to [Note: $\operatorname{adj}M$ denotes the adjoint of a square matrix $M$ and $[k]$ denotes the largest integer less than or equal to $k$]. [JEE-2010]
questions.key_idea: $\det(\operatorname{adj}M)=(\det M)^2$ for $3\times3$; $B$ is skew-symmetric of odd order so $\det B=0$.
solution: $\det A=\begin{vmatrix}2k-1&2\sqrt k&2\sqrt k\\2\sqrt k&1&-2k\\-2\sqrt k&2k&-1\end{vmatrix}$. Apply $C_2\to C_2-C_3$.
$=\begin{vmatrix}2k-1&0&2\sqrt k\\4\sqrt k&0&1-2k\\-2\sqrt k&2k+1&-1\end{vmatrix}$. Expand along $C_2$: $\det A=(2k+1)\cdot(2k+1)^2=(2k+1)^3$.
$B$ is skew-symmetric (its $(i,j)$ and $(j,i)$ entries are negatives and the diagonal is $0$) of odd order $3$, so $\det B=0$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Each row of $A$ has the same length $2k+1$ and the rows are mutually perpendicular, so $\frac{A}{2k+1}$ is orthogonal.
solution: Dot products: $R_1\cdot R_2=(2k-1)2\sqrt k+2\sqrt k-4k\sqrt k=0$, and similarly $R_1\cdot R_3=0$, $R_2\cdot R_3=0$.
So $\frac A{2k+1}$ is orthogonal, $\det\frac A{2k+1}=\pm1$, i.e. $\det A=\pm(2k+1)^3$.
The sign is constant for $k\ge0$ (the determinant never vanishes) and at $k=0$: $A=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,-1)$ has $\det=+1$. So $\det A=(2k+1)^3$.
Then $(2k+1)^6=10^6$ gives $k=4.5$ and $[k]=4$ (with $\det B=0$ as before). Same answer.

useful_results: $\det(\operatorname{adj}M)=(\det M)^{n-1}$; for $n=3$ it is $(\det M)^2$, always $\ge0$.
A real skew-symmetric matrix of odd order has determinant $0$ since $|B|=|B^T|=|-B|=(-1)^n|B|$.
If the rows of $A$ are pairwise perpendicular with the same length $r$, then $|\det A|=r^n$.
Use row/column operations that create zeros before expanding; here $C_2-C_3$ and $R_2-R_3$ do it.

concepts: Evaluation of a $2\times2$ determinant
Prime factorisation of an integer
questions.paragraph: Consider $N=\begin{vmatrix}77&44\\7&30\end{vmatrix}=\prod_{i=1}^{4}(a_i)^{b_i}$, where $b_i\in\mathbb N$ and the $a_i$ are prime numbers with $a_i<a_{i+1}$ for all $i$. Two circles are defined as $C_1:\ \begin{bmatrix}x^2&y^2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}a_1\\b_1+b_2\end{bmatrix}=[8b_1]$ and $C_2:\ \begin{bmatrix}(x+y)^2&(x-y)^2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}b_3\\b_4\end{bmatrix}=[2b_2]$.
questions.question: The value $\sum_{i=1}^{4}(a_i+b_i)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: $N=2002=2\cdot7\cdot11\cdot13$ has four distinct primes, so every exponent $b_i$ is $1$.
solution: $2002=2\times7\times11\times13$: four distinct primes, and $N$ is a product of four prime powers with $a_1<a_2<a_3<a_4$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Take the common factor $7$ out of the first column to get $N=7\times286$ and factorise at once.
solution: $286=2\times143=2\times11\times13$, so $N=2\times7\times11\times13$: four distinct primes, hence all $b_i=1$.

useful_results: A common factor of a row or column can be taken outside a determinant: $\begin{vmatrix}kp&q\\kr&s\end{vmatrix}=k\begin{vmatrix}p&q\\r&s\end{vmatrix}$.
Unique prime factorisation: if $N$ equals a product of $4$ prime powers and has exactly $4$ distinct prime factors, each exponent is the exact power in $N$.
Useful: $1001=7\times11\times13$ and so $2002=2\times1001$, $3003=3\times1001$, ...
A paragraph question: record the values $a_i,b_i$ once; all later parts reuse them.

concepts: Matrix multiplication as an equation of a circle
Circle touching another circle
questions.paragraph: Consider $N=\begin{vmatrix}77&44\\7&30\end{vmatrix}=\prod_{i=1}^{4}(a_i)^{b_i}$, where $b_i\in\mathbb N$ and the $a_i$ are prime numbers with $a_i<a_{i+1}$ for all $i$. Two circles are defined as $C_1:\ \begin{bmatrix}x^2&y^2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}a_1\\b_1+b_2\end{bmatrix}=[8b_1]$ and $C_2:\ \begin{bmatrix}(x+y)^2&(x-y)^2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}b_3\\b_4\end{bmatrix}=[2b_2]$.
questions.question: Radius of the circle which passes through the centre of the circle $C_2$ and touches the circle $C_1$ is:
questions.key_idea: With all $b_i=1$ both circles are centred at the origin, and a circle through the origin touching $C_1$ internally has the radius $\frac R2$.
solution: The required circle passes through $O$ (the centre of $C_2$ and also of $C_1$) and touches $C_1$, which has radius $2$.
It touches $C_1$ at a point $T$ with $OT=2$; $O$ and $T$ both lie on it and on a line through its centre, so $OT$ is a diameter: $2r=2$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Coordinate method: a circle through the origin has its centre at distance $r$ from $O$, and internal tangency with $C_1$ needs $d=R-r$.
solution: Let the required circle have radius $r$ and centre $Q$. It passes through $O$, so $OQ=r$.

$C_1$ has radius $R=2$ and centre $O$. $O$ is inside the required circle's boundary (on it), so the circles touch internally: $OQ=R-r$ (a circle through the centre of $C_1$ cannot touch it externally).

useful_results: $\begin{bmatrix}x^2&y^2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}p\\q\end{bmatrix}=[c]$ means $px^2+qy^2=c$: a circle if $p=q$ (radius $\sqrt{c/p}$).
A circle through the centre of a circle of radius $R$ and touching it has radius $\frac R2$ (the two circles touch internally at the far end of a diameter).
Tangency of circles: $d=r_1+r_2$ (external) or $d=|r_1-r_2|$ (internal).
$(x+y)^2+(x-y)^2=2(x^2+y^2)$ — a quick identity for such expressions.

concepts: Family of lines through a fixed point
Length of tangent from a point to a circle
questions.paragraph: Consider $N=\begin{vmatrix}77&44\\7&30\end{vmatrix}=\prod_{i=1}^{4}(a_i)^{b_i}$, where $b_i\in\mathbb N$ and the $a_i$ are prime numbers with $a_i<a_{i+1}$ for all $i$. Two circles are defined as $C_1:\ \begin{bmatrix}x^2&y^2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}a_1\\b_1+b_2\end{bmatrix}=[8b_1]$ and $C_2:\ \begin{bmatrix}(x+y)^2&(x-y)^2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}b_3\\b_4\end{bmatrix}=[2b_2]$.
questions.question: If the line $x+\lambda y=1+k\lambda$ always passes through a fixed point on the circle $C_1$ for all values of $\lambda$, then the length of the tangent from the point $\left(1,\sqrt3k\right)$ to the circle $C_2$ is:
questions.key_idea: $x-1+\lambda(y-k)=0$ passes through $(1,k)$ for every $\lambda$; that point lies on $C_1$, so $k^2=3$.
solution: For all $\lambda$ the line passes through $L_1=0,L_2=0$, i.e. the fixed point $(1,k)$.
Length of the tangent $=\sqrt{S_1}=\sqrt{1+9-1}=3=k^2$. So the answer is (B).

alternate_solutions.idea: Keep $k$ symbolic: the squared tangent length from $(1,\sqrt3k)$ is $3k^2$, and $k^2=3$ turns $\sqrt{3k^2}=\sqrt3|k|$ into $k^2$.
solution: The fixed point is $(1,k)$, and $1+k^2=4$ gives $k^2=3$.
Power of $(1,\sqrt3k)$ with respect to $C_2$: $S_1=1+3k^2-1=3k^2$, so the tangent length is $\sqrt{3k^2}=\sqrt3|k|$.

Since $|k|=\sqrt3$: $\sqrt3|k|=\sqrt3\cdot\sqrt3=3$, and $k^2=3$, so the length equals $k^2$. Check the others: $k=\pm\sqrt3
eq3$, $2k=\pm2\sqrt3
eq3$, $2k^2=6
eq3$. Same answer (B).

useful_results: A family $L_1+\lambda L_2=0$ passes through the fixed point $L_1=0\cap L_2=0$ for every $\lambda$.
Length of tangent from $(x_1,y_1)$ to $x^2+y^2=r^2$ is $\sqrt{x_1^2+y_1^2-r^2}$ (zero on the circle, imaginary inside).
For the option check, evaluate each option at $k^2=3$: only $k^2$ equals $3$.
Read earlier parts of a paragraph for the data: here $a_1=2$ fixes $C_1:x^2+y^2=4$.

concepts: Symmetric matrices
Counting by combinations
questions.paragraph: Let $\mathcal A$ be the set of all $3\times3$ symmetric matrices all of whose entries are either $0$ or $1$. Five of these entries are $1$ and four of them are $0$.
questions.question: The number of matrices in $\mathcal A$ is: [JEE-2009]
questions.key_idea: In a symmetric matrix an off-diagonal $1$ comes in a pair, so the number of $1$s on the diagonal is odd (1 or 3).
solution: A symmetric matrix is fixed by its three diagonal entries and three off-diagonal entries $a_{12},a_{13},a_{23}$; each off-diagonal entry occupies two places.
Total number of $1$s is $5$ (odd), so the number of $1$s on the diagonal is odd: it is $3$ or $1$.
Case I: all three diagonal entries are $1$. The other two $1$s form one off-diagonal pair: ${}^3C_1=3$ matrices.

Case II: one diagonal entry is $1$ (the other two are $0$) and two off-diagonal pairs are $1$s ($1+4=5$). Number $={}^3C_1\cdot{}^3C_1=9$ (choose the diagonal $1$, then the off-diagonal pair that is $0$).
useful_results: Symmetric $n\times n$ matrices are determined by $\frac{n(n+1)}2$ entries; off-diagonal entries count twice in totals like 'number of $1$s'.
Parity trick: sum of entries $=$ (diagonal sum) $+2\times$ (off-diagonal sum), so the diagonal sum has the same parity as the total.
Symmetric $0$–$1$ matrices correspond to graphs with loops allowed; a loop adds $1$ to the total, an edge adds $2$.
Verify counts by brute force on small cases (here $2^6=64$ matrices in all).

concepts: Determinant and unique solution of a linear system
Counting of symmetric $0$–$1$ matrices
questions.paragraph: Let $\mathcal A$ be the set of all $3\times3$ symmetric matrices all of whose entries are either $0$ or $1$. Five of these entries are $1$ and four of them are $0$.
questions.question: The number of matrices $A$ in $\mathcal A$ for which the system of linear equations $A\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\\z\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\0\end{pmatrix}$ has a unique solution is: [JEE-2009]
questions.key_idea: A unique solution needs $\det A\neq0$; test the two types (three diagonal $1$s, or one diagonal $1$) with the $3\times3$ symmetric determinant.
solution: A unique solution of $A\mathbf x=(1,0,0)^T$ exists iff $\det A\neq0$.
Case I (all diagonal entries $1$): $\det A=\begin{vmatrix}1&a&b\\a&1&c\\b&c&1\end{vmatrix}=1-a^2-b^2-c^2+2abc$ with $(a,b,c)$ a permutation of $(1,0,0)$.
Then $\det A=1-1=0$ in all three arrangements, so no matrix works in Case I.
Case II (i): $\det\begin{vmatrix}1&a&b\\a&0&c\\b&c&0\end{vmatrix}=2abc-c^2$ with $(a,b,c)$ a permutation of $(1,1,0)$: non-zero only if $c=1$, which gives $2$ matrices.
Case II (ii): $\det\begin{vmatrix}0&a&b\\a&1&c\\b&c&0\end{vmatrix}=2abc-b^2$: non-zero only if $b=1$: $2$ matrices.
Case II (iii): $\det\begin{vmatrix}0&a&b\\a&0&c\\b&c&1\end{vmatrix}=2abc-a^2$: non-zero only if $a=1$: $2$ matrices.
Hence exactly $6$ matrices give a unique solution: option (B).

alternate_solutions.idea: Read the matrix as a graph (a loop at one vertex and two edges); equal rows make the determinant $0$, so only one configuration survives.
solution: Case I: $A=I+E$ where $E$ has a single symmetric pair of $1$s at $(i,j)$. Then rows $i$ and $j$ are both $e_i+e_j$ — equal — so $\det A=0$. None of these $3$ matrices works.
Case II: the two $1$-pairs form a path $u-m-v$ with centre $m$, and the diagonal $1$ is at one vertex.
If the diagonal $1$ is at the centre $m$: the rows of $u$ and $v$ are both $e_m$, so they are equal and $\det A=0$ (3 matrices).

If the diagonal $1$ is at an end, say $u$: e.g. $\begin{pmatrix}1&1&0\\1&0&1\\0&1&0\end{pmatrix}$ has $\det=-1\neq0$ (expand along the last row). There are $3$ centres $\times\,2$ ends $=6$ such matrices.
So exactly $6$ matrices have $\det A\neq0$: option (B). Same answer.

useful_results: $3\times3$ symmetric: $\det\begin{pmatrix}p&a&b\\a&q&c\\b&c&r\end{pmatrix}=pqr+2abc-pc^2-qb^2-ra^2$.
Two equal rows (or columns) $\Rightarrow\det=0$; for $0$–$1$ symmetric matrices check this before expanding.
$A\mathbf x=\mathbf b$ has a unique solution $\iff\det A\neq0$ (for every $\mathbf b$).
Counting pattern: classify by the diagonal first, then the off-diagonal pairs.

concepts: Consistency of a system (inconsistent systems)
Counting of symmetric $0$–$1$ matrices
questions.paragraph: Let $\mathcal A$ be the set of all $3\times3$ symmetric matrices all of whose entries are either $0$ or $1$. Five of these entries are $1$ and four of them are $0$.
questions.question: The number of matrices $A$ in $\mathcal A$ for which the system of linear equations $A\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\\z\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\0\end{pmatrix}$ is inconsistent is: [JEE-2009]
questions.key_idea: Write the three equations $x+ay+bz=1$, etc.; find three or more matrices whose equations contradict each other.
solution: Case I (diagonal $1,1,1$): $x+ay+bz=1$, $ax+y+cz=0$, $bx+cy+z=0$, with $(a,b,c)$ a permutation of $(1,0,0)$.
Case II, with $(a,b,c)$ a permutation of $(1,1,0)$ and one diagonal $1$: for the diagonal $1$ at the first place all three arrangements are consistent.
Diagonal $1$ at the middle place with $b=0$, $a=c=1$: $y+0\cdot z=1$, $x+y+z=0$, $y=0$ — $y=1$ and $y=0$ contradict: inconsistent.

So at least three matrices (two in Case I, one in Case II) give an inconsistent system: more than $2$, option (B). (Checking the remaining case, $a_{33}=1$ with $a_{13}=a_{23}=1$, gives a fourth one: exactly $4$.)

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the structure from Q21: a singular matrix with two equal rows gives an inconsistent system exactly when the right-hand sides of those two rows differ.
solution: The $6$ matrices with $\det A\neq0$ (Q21) give a unique solution, so only the other $6$ can be inconsistent.

Case I ($I$ plus a pair at $(i,j)$): rows $i,j$ are equal. The right-hand side $(1,0,0)$ has different entries in rows $i,j$ exactly when the pair includes row $1$: pairs $(1,2)$ and $(1,3)$ give inconsistent systems; $(2,3)$ is consistent. Count: $2$.

Case II (diagonal $1$ at the centre $m$ of the path $u-m-v$): the rows of $u,v$ are equal ($=e_m$) and the system is inconsistent iff the right-hand side differs on rows $u,v$, i.e. iff $1\in\{u,v\}$.
For $m=2$ ($u,v=1,3$) and $m=3$ ($u,v=1,2$) the system is inconsistent; for $m=1$ ($u,v=2,3$) it is consistent. Count: $2$.

useful_results: A system with two identical rows is inconsistent iff the right-hand-side entries in those rows differ.
$A\mathbf x=\mathbf b$ is consistent iff $\mathbf b\in$ column space of $A$; for symmetric $A$ this is iff $\mathbf b\perp\ker A$.
When $\det A=0$ test consistency with rank: $\operatorname{rank}[A|\mathbf b]>\operatorname{rank}A$ means inconsistent.
Unique / none / infinite classification of all twelve matrices here: $6$ unique, $4$ none, $2$ infinite.

concepts: Symmetric and skew-symmetric matrices
Divisibility by a prime (counting modulo $p$)
questions.paragraph: Let $p$ be an odd prime number and $T_p$ be the following set of $2\times2$ matrices: $T_p=\left\{A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&a\end{pmatrix}:a,b,c\in\{0,1,2,\ldots,p-1\}\right\}$.
questions.question: The number of $A$ in $T_p$ such that $A$ is either symmetric or skew-symmetric or both, and $\det(A)$ is divisible by $p$ is: [JEE-2010]
questions.key_idea: Symmetric means $b=c$, so $\det A=a^2-b^2=(a-b)(a+b)$; count pairs with $a\equiv\pm b\pmod p$.
solution: $A$ skew-symmetric: $A^T=-A\Rightarrow a=-a$ and $b+c=0$, so $a=0$; since $b,c\ge0$, $b=c=0$. This is the zero matrix, which is also symmetric.
So we need symmetric matrices ($b=c$) with $\det A=a^2-bc=a^2-b^2=(a-b)(a+b)$ divisible by $p$.
As $p$ is prime, $p\mid(a-b)$ or $p\mid(a+b)$. Since $0\le a,b\le p-1$: $a-b$ lies in $[-(p-1),p-1]$, whose only multiple of $p$ is $0$: $a=b$ gives $p$ pairs.
$a+b$ lies in $[0,2p-2]$, whose multiples of $p$ are $0$ and $p$. $a+b=0$ gives $a=b=0$ (already counted); $a+b=p$ gives $a=1,\ldots,p-1$ with $b=p-a$: $p-1$ pairs (none has $a=b$, as $p$ is odd).
questions.correction_note: PDF says the range 0..2p-2 of (a+b) 'includes only one multiple of p, i.e. p'. It also contains 0 (a=b=0). That case is already inside a = b, so the final count 2p-1 is right, but the statement is wrong; the pair (0,0) is now explicitly accounted for. Verified by brute force for p = 3, 5, 7, 11.

alternate_solutions.idea: Work in the field $\mathbb F_p$: $a^2=b^2$ is a pair of lines $a=b$ and $a=-b$ through the origin of the $(a,b)$-plane, each with $p$ points.
solution: In $\mathbb F_p$, $a^2-b^2=(a-b)(a+b)=0\iff a=b$ or $a=-b$: two lines through the origin of the plane $\mathbb F_p^2$.
Each line has $p$ points, and the lines meet only at the origin $(0,0)$ (since $a=b=-b$ forces $b=0$ for odd $p$).
Number of pairs $(a,b)=p+p-1=2p-1$, and for each pair $c=b$ is fixed. Same answer (D).

useful_results: For a prime $p$: $p\mid xy\iff p\mid x$ or $p\mid y$.
Over $\mathbb F_p$ with $p$ odd, $x^2=y^2\iff y=\pm x$: exactly $2p-1$ solutions $(x,y)$.
A matrix that is both symmetric and skew-symmetric is $O$; real skew-symmetric matrices have zero diagonal.
When entries are restricted to $0\ldots p-1$ list the possible values of $a\pm b$ and count multiples of $p$ carefully, including $0$.

questions.paragraph: Let $p$ be an odd prime number and $T_p$ be the following set of $2\times2$ matrices: $T_p=\left\{A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&a\end{pmatrix}:a,b,c\in\{0,1,2,\ldots,p-1\}\right\}$.
questions.question: The number of $A$ in $T_p$ such that the trace of $A$ is not divisible by $p$ but $\det(A)$ is divisible by $p$ is: [Note: the trace of a matrix is the sum of its diagonal entries.] [JEE-2010]
questions.key_idea:
$\operatorname{tr}A=2a
ot\equiv0$ means $a
eq0$; then $bc\equiv a^2
ot\equiv0$ fixes $c$ once $b
eq0$ is chosen.
solution: $\operatorname{tr}A=2a$, and $p$ is an odd prime, so $p\nmid2a\iff a\neq0$: $a$ can be chosen in $p-1$ ways.
$\det A=a^2-bc$ is divisible by $p$: $bc\equiv a^2\pmod p$.

For each such $b$ there is exactly one $c\in\{0,\ldots,p-1\}$ with $bc\equiv a^2\pmod p$, because $b$ has an inverse modulo $p$ (e.g. $p=5$, $a=4$: $a^2\equiv1$, pairs $(b,c)=(1,1),(2,3),(3,2),(4,4)$).
useful_results: Modulo a prime $p$, every non-zero $b$ has a unique inverse, so $bc\equiv t$ ($t\not\equiv0$) has exactly $p-1$ solutions $(b,c)$ with $b,c\in\{1,\ldots,p-1\}$.
For $p$ odd, $2a\equiv0\iff a\equiv0$: halving is safe modulo an odd prime.
Number of solutions of $bc\equiv0$: $b=0$ or $c=0$, i.e. $2p-1$.
Check small cases: $p=3$ gives $4$ matrices (brute force confirms $(p-1)^2=4$).

questions.paragraph: Let $p$ be an odd prime number and $T_p$ be the following set of $2\times2$ matrices: $T_p=\left\{A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&a\end{pmatrix}:a,b,c\in\{0,1,2,\ldots,p-1\}\right\}$.
questions.question: The number of $A$ in $T_p$ such that $\det(A)$ is not divisible by $p$ is: [JEE-2010]
questions.key_idea: Count the complement: the matrices with $p\mid\det A$ are $(p-1)^2$ with $a\neq0$ plus $2p-1$ with $a=0$, in total $p^2$.
solution: Total number of matrices in $T_p$ is $p^3$ ($a,b,c$ each have $p$ values).
When $a\neq0$ and $\det A$ is divisible by $p$, the number of matrices is $(p-1)^2$ (Q24, without the trace condition: it is automatic).
When $a=0$ and $\det A=-bc$ is divisible by $p$: $bc\equiv0$, so $b=0$ or $c=0$: $p+p-1=2p-1$ matrices.
Total matrices with $\det A$ divisible by $p$ $=(p-1)^2+2p-1=p^2$.
So the number with $\det A$ not divisible by $p$ is $p^3-p^2$: option (D).

alternate_solutions.idea: Count the $(b,c)$ for which $a^2=bc$ is solvable using the Legendre symbol: $a$ has $1+\left(\frac{bc}p\right)$ solutions, and the symbol sums to $0$.
solution: Fix $(b,c)$. The number of $a\in\mathbb F_p$ with $a^2=bc$ is $1+\chi(bc)$, where $\chi$ is the Legendre symbol ($\chi(0)=0$, $\chi=\pm1$ for residues/non-residues).
$\sum_b\chi(b)=0$ (equally many residues and non-residues), so the number is $p^2$.
Hence the number with $\det A$ not divisible by $p$ is $p^3-p^2$. Same answer (D).

useful_results: Number of solutions of $a^2\equiv t\pmod p$ is $1+\chi(t)$, with $\chi$ the Legendre symbol; $\sum_{t=0}^{p-1}\chi(t)=0$.
Complement counting: count the singular ones, subtract from the total.
Over $\mathbb F_p$, the singular matrices of this form number $p^2$, i.e. the surface $a^2=bc$ (a cone) has $p^2$ points.

useful_results: $\mathbf x^TM=0$ has a non-zero solution iff $\det M=0$; then the solutions form a line (rank $2$) through the origin.
For a rank-$2$ homogeneous $3\times3$ system the solution direction is the cross product of two independent rows (or columns).
Here the whole solution set is $(a,b,c)=t(1,6,-7)$; the sum of the coordinates is $0$, matching (iii).

questions.question: Let $\omega$ be a solution of $x^3-1=0$ with $\operatorname{Im}(\omega)>0$. If $a=2$ with $b$ and $c$ satisfying (E), then the value of $\frac3{\omega^a}+\frac1{\omega^b}+\frac3{\omega^c}$ is equal to: [JEE-2011]

The solution of (E) is $(a,b,c)=t(1,6,-7)$: for $a=2$ take $t=2$ giving $(2,12,-14)$.

questions.question: Let $b=6$, with $a$ and $c$ satisfying (E). If $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the roots of the quadratic equation $ax^2+bx+c=0$, then $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\left(\frac1\alpha+\frac1\beta\right)^n$ is: [JEE-2011]
questions.key_idea: $\frac1\alpha+\frac1\beta=-\frac bc=\frac67$, so the series is an infinite G.P. with ratio $\frac67$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use $(a,b,c)=t(1,6,-7)$ and Vieta's formulas, without solving the quadratic.
solution: The G.P. sum is $\frac1{1-6/7}=7$. Same answer (B).

A quadratic whose coefficients sum to $0$ (here $1+6-7=0$) has $x=1$ as a root.
$\sum_{n\ge0}r^n=\frac1{1-r}$ for $|r|<1$; check $|r|<1$ before using it.
The family $(a,b,c)=t(1,6,-7)$ answers Q26–Q28 with one idea.

questions.question:
Consider the matrices $A= egin{pmatrix}3&-4\1&-1\end{pmatrix}$ and $B= egin{pmatrix}a&b\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ and let $P$ be any orthogonal matrix and $Q=PAP^T$ and $R=P^TQ^KP$, also $S=PBP^T$ and $T=P^TS^KP$.
Column I
(A) If we vary $K$ from $1$ to $n$, then the first row first column elements of $R$ will form
(B) If we vary $K$ from $1$ to $n$, then the 2nd row 2nd column elements of $R$ will form
(C) If we vary $K$ from $1$ to $n$, then the first row first column elements of $T$ will form
(D) If we vary $K$ from $3$ to $n$, then the first row 2nd column elements of $T$ will represent the sum of
Column II
(P) G.P. with common ratio $a$
(Q) A.P. with common difference $2$
(R) G.P. with common ratio $b$
(S) A.P. with common difference $-2$
questions.key_idea: Orthogonality cancels the conjugation: $R=P^T(PAP^T)^KP=A^K$ and $T=B^K$.
solution: (A) $R=A^K$: first row first column entries $3,5,7,\ldots$ form an A.P. with common difference $2$: (A) $\to$ Q.
(B) second row second column entries $-1,-3,-5,\ldots$: A.P. with common difference $-2$: (B) $\to$ S.
(C) $T=B^K$: first row first column entries $a,a^2,a^3,\ldots$: G.P. with common ratio $a$: (C) $\to$ P.
(D) The first row second column entry of $B^K$ is $b(1+a+a^2+\cdots+a^{K-1})$: the sum of a G.P. with common ratio $a$: (D) $\to$ P.

alternate_solutions.idea: Write $A=I+N$ with $N^2=O$, so $A^K=I+KN$ exactly; for $B^K$ use the recurrence of the $(1,2)$ entry.
solution: $I$ and $N$ commute, so $A^K=I+KN=\begin{pmatrix}2K+1&-4K\\K&1-2K\end{pmatrix}$ (binomial theorem with all terms beyond the second zero).
So $T_{11}=a^K$ is a G.P. with ratio $a$ (C) P, and $T_{12}=b(1+a+\cdots+a^{K-1})$ is a G.P. sum with ratio $a$ (D) P. Same answers.

useful_results: If $P$ is orthogonal then $(PAP^T)^K=PA^KP^T$ and $P^T(PAP^T)^KP=A^K$: similarity by an orthogonal (or any invertible) matrix commutes with powers.
If $N^2=O$ then $(I+N)^K=I+KN$; for $A=\begin{pmatrix}3&-4\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}$ (trace $2$, det $1$, eigenvalue $1$ repeated) this gives $A^K=\begin{pmatrix}2K+1&-4K\\K&1-2K\end{pmatrix}$.
$\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\0&1\end{pmatrix}^K=\begin{pmatrix}a^K&b\frac{a^K-1}{a-1}\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ for $a\neq1$.
Matrices with repeated eigenvalue $1$ and $(A-I)^2=O$ have powers that are linear in $K$ (an A.P.) in every entry.

questions.question:
Consider a square matrix $A$ of order $2$ which has its elements as $0,1,2$ and $4$ (all four elements different). Let $N$ denote the number of such matrices.
Column A
(A) Possible non-negative value of $\det(A)$ is
(B) Sum of values of determinants corresponding to $N$ matrices is
(C) If the absolute value of $\det(A)$ is least, then possible value of $|\operatorname{adj}(\operatorname{adj}(\operatorname{adj}A))|$ is
(D) If $\det(A)$ is algebraically least, then possible value of $\det(4A^{-1})$ is
Column B
(P) $2$ (Q) $4$ (R) $-2$ (S) $0$ (T) $8$
questions.answer: (A) P, Q, T; (B) S; (C) P, R; (D) R
questions.key_idea: The four elements are a permutation of $0,1,2,4$, so $N=24$ and $\det=ad-bc$ takes the values $\pm2,\pm4,\pm8$ (each sign equally often).
solution: All four entries are different, so the matrices correspond to the $4!=24$ arrangements of $0,1,2,4$: $N=24$.

(A) Examples: $\begin{vmatrix}2&4\\0&1\end{vmatrix}=2$, $\begin{vmatrix}4&2\\0&1\end{vmatrix}=4$, $\begin{vmatrix}4&1\\0&2\end{vmatrix}=8$. The non-negative values are $2,4,8$: P, Q, T ($0$ never occurs, because $ad=bc$ is impossible when one product is $0$ and the other is not).
(B) The possible values of $\det A$ are $\pm2,\pm4,\pm8$; interchanging two rows changes the sign, so the $24$ matrices pair off into $+$/$-$ pairs and the sum $=0$: S.
(C) The least absolute value of $\det A$ is $2$, so $\det A=\pm2$.

For $n=2$, $\operatorname{adj}(\operatorname{adj}M)=M$, so $\operatorname{adj}(\operatorname{adj}(\operatorname{adj}A))=\operatorname{adj}A$ and $|\operatorname{adj}A|=|A|^{2-1}=\pm2$ (in general $|\operatorname{adj}^kA|=|A|^{(n-1)^k}=|A|$ for $n=2$): P, R.
(D) The algebraically least determinant is $-8$ (for $\begin{pmatrix}0&4\\2&1\end{pmatrix}$ etc.).
questions.correction_note: PDF part (C) quotes |adj(adj(A))| = |A|^((2-1)^2) = +-2, a formula for two adjoints; the question has three. For n = 2 the exponent (n-1)^k = 1 for every k, so the value (+-2) is the same; the working was rewritten for three adjoints. Matrices are taken to have all four elements different (as in the Hindi text; N = 24).

alternate_solutions.idea: Pair up the four numbers: $\det=ad-bc$ is the difference of the products of two complementary pairs, and there are only three ways to split $\{0,1,2,4\}$ into two pairs.
solution: A matrix uses the diagonal pair $\{a,d\}$ and the off-diagonal pair $\{b,c\}$; these two pairs split $\{0,1,2,4\}$ in one of $3$ ways.
Each split gives $8$ matrices ($2$ choices of which pair is on the diagonal $\times$ $2\times2$ orders): $24$ in all, with $\det=+k$ and $-k$ equally often.

(A) Non-negative values: $2,4,8$ (P, Q, T). (B) Sum $=0$ by the $\pm$ symmetry (S). (C) $|\det|_{\min}=2$, and $|\operatorname{adj}^3A|=|A|^{1}=\pm2$ (P, R). (D) Least $\det=-8$, so $\det(4A^{-1})=\frac{16}{-8}=-2$ (R). Same answers.

useful_results: For a $2\times2$ matrix: $\operatorname{adj}(\operatorname{adj}A)=A$, $\operatorname{adj}A=\begin{pmatrix}d&-b\\-c&a\end{pmatrix}$ and $\det(\operatorname{adj}A)=\det A$.
In general $|\operatorname{adj}A|=|A|^{n-1}$ and $|\operatorname{adj}^kA|=|A|^{(n-1)^k}$; $\det(cA)=c^n\det A$; $\det(A^{-1})=\frac1{\det A}$.
Swapping the two rows of a matrix negates its determinant, so sets of matrices closed under row swapping have determinant sum $0$.
For matrices built from distinct numbers $\{w,x,y,z\}$: $\det=\pm(\text{product of pair}-\text{product of complementary pair})$ over $3$ pairings.
